commit.message:
Run over riders on foot instead of riding through them

A rider who had come off and was running back to the bike, or lying where
they landed, took no part in any collision: every check in the sim was
between two riders on bikes, so a bike went straight through them with
nothing seen or heard. Ledger C9 had sat at planned since the first plan.

The recording shows it once, at about 20 km/h (317.56-318.80): the walker
is thrown up spread-eagled on the frame of contact, about a metre up with a
shadow under them, off to the side and back past the camera within 0.4 s;
the bike that hit them is in the air for four frames, then goes over hard
and rocks back, and its rider stays on. A bike ridden into someone on foot
now throws them that way, hops, tilts away after the hop, is checked to
85% of its speed and makes its own thud. One's own bike feels it the moment
it reaches them, not a round trip later.

The first throw sent the walker on at 0.55 of the bike's speed and 3 m/s
sideways. Played headless at 1280x720 on the GPU, it went on ahead and was
hidden behind the rider who hit it; at 0.3 and 6 m/s it goes off to the
side and back, as in the recording.

spec/ram.test.ts rides at a rider jogging back to a bike, and at one lying
in the road, through the whole server-to-browser path: each run over once.
With the run-over switched off, those two and both new tests in
spec/touch.test.ts fail. In the real game a bot sent after riders on foot
ran over 9 in 60 s, every one reported by the server.

107 tests across 15 files green.

commit.message:
Add a minimal PNG codec, and a tools area to put it in (#97)

* Add a minimal PNG codec, and a tools area to put it in

`adb exec-out screencap -p` hands back a PNG and Tesseract wants one, so
reading a phone's screen needs a codec at both ends. A dependency would
do it, but the whole of what is needed is an 8-bit non-interlaced image
in one of the four colour types a phone produces, and `node:zlib`
already carries the inflate, the deflate and the CRC.

What this adds beyond the decode and encode is the handful of
transformations the readers above it will want: a clamped crop that can
invert as it goes, a nearest-neighbour enlargement, two thresholds and a
banded frame difference. Each is a pure function of a pixel buffer, so
the test builds its own images and needs no phone, no screenshot and no
Tesseract.

`src/tools/` is new, and it gets its own runner rather than joining the
fast suite: the modules that follow reach `node:child_process`, and
their tests will read committed screenshots at about four seconds each,
which is not something to put in a suite that runs in half a second.
`test` excludes the directory and `test:inventory` is what collects it.

The two thresholds are the pair worth reading together. `isolate` keeps
a pixel only where it is both bright and grey, and `brighten` keeps it
for being bright alone, so the same cyan is deleted by one and kept by
the other — which is why PGSharp's overlay gets read both ways. Both
tests use cyan rather than the magenta that overlay actually draws,
because magenta's luminance is 72.6 and fails the floor before the
colour test is ever reached: with magenta, deleting the chroma bound
entirely leaves both tests passing. Measured rather than assumed, by
making that deletion and watching them pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01N78kMxFhWp2KWsooyATs1w

* Read text off a screenshot with the Tesseract CLI (#98)

Pokémon GO is drawn by Unity, so there is no view hierarchy to ask:
`uiautomator dump` sees one opaque surface and the pixels are all there
is. This wraps the Tesseract CLI, which has to be installed separately
at 4.1 or later, and groups its TSV rows into lines positioned in the
pixels of the image read — so readers can anchor on where text sits
wherever the screen gives them something to anchor on, rather than on
fixed coordinates. The game lays itself out differently on every aspect
ratio, and "the line above the HP" holds on all of them where
"y = 1180" holds on one.

Two modes, and the difference between them is not small. `ocr` uses page
segmentation mode 11, sparse text, because a game screen is labels
scattered over artwork rather than a page of paragraphs. `ocrLine` uses
mode 7 for a caller that has already cropped to something it knows the
shape of, and answers only the text: a band holding `L1 IV48 5/2/15`
over a bright background reads as `r '` sparse and as `L1 1V48 5/2/15`
as a line, because sparse mode takes the blocks either side of it for
pictures rather than for the margins they are.

Tesseract is run through one helper so that what it needs is said once:
TSV through `tessedit_create_tsv` rather than a config file a
models-only install lacks, OpenMP held to one thread so that reads run
side by side do not spin-wait against each other, an EPIPE on stdin
left to the exit status to explain rather than killing Node, and a
SIGFPE, which some whitelisted bands cause every time, counted as
nothing read.

`ocr.test.mts` pins `findLine`, `centre` and `fold`, which have no
reader below the CLI, and a Tesseract failing to start under an image
too big for the pipe. Reading real captures is left to the readers that
have them a few commits along.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Trim a crop at the image's edges rather than sliding it inside

A negative origin was clamped to zero with the width left as it was,
so `crop(image, -2, 0, 3, 1)` answered columns 0–2 where only column 0
overlaps, and `line.left - pad` or `hp.top - hp.height * 4` further up
the stack picked up pixels on the far side they never asked for. An
origin at or past the right edge was worse: `Math.max(1, …)` forced
the width up to one, and the copy ran on into the next row.

The rectangle is now intersected with the image, and one wholly
outside it is empty. The floor of one pixel was what kept such a crop
away from Tesseract, which refuses a PNG with no width or height as
`Invalid IHDR data`, so `tesseract` answers an empty image as having
no text rather than failing the scan over it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Refuse a damaged or cut-off PNG rather than decode it

A `screencap` stream cut off after its signature threw a raw
`RangeError` from reading a chunk header past the end, or zlib's
`unexpected end of file` inside the IDAT, and a damaged one decoded
without complaint: an unknown filter byte was read as filter 0, short
inflate output was padded out with zeros by `?? 0`, and no CRC was
checked. A valid signature followed by IDAT and IEND decoded to a 0×0
image. Each of these is now refused by name, with the same pointer
at `screencap` the signature check gives.

The old "truncated" test dropped the first byte, which broke the
signature and never tested truncation at all; it is now named for what
it does, beside one that cuts the stream at six points after the
signature.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Share one threshold loop between `isolate` and `brighten`

`brighten` repeated the whole of `isolate`'s loop — allocate, test,
write black or white, alpha 255 — with only the per-pixel test
changed. Each now says only its test, so the two cannot drift apart
on the rest.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Spell the tools directory the same way in the type check and both suites

`scripts/tsconfig.json` checked `src/tools/inventory/*.mts` while
`test:inventory` collects all of `src/tools`, so a module at
`src/tools/<other>/x.mts` or `src/tools/inventory/sub/x.mts` would run
without ever being type-checked. It now claims `src/tools/**/*.mts`.

`test` excluded `**/tools/**`, which would also have silently dropped
a future `src/map/tools/` from the fast suite. Vitest matches
`--exclude` against `--dir`, so `tools/**` names `src/tools/` and
nothing else; a probe test at `src/zz/tools/` is collected by `test`
and one at `src/tools/zz/` by `test:inventory` and the type check.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Count a pixel as changed in `difference` when any channel moves

It compared the red channel alone, so (0,1,2) turning to (0,255,255)
scored zero, and blue or cyan text appearing on a dark panel would
read as a screen that had settled. Its doc comment said that answered
the same question, and had come loose above `brighten`'s, leaving one
function with two and the other with none.

The panel figures in the comment were measured against red alone, so
they stay as a floor for the new measure rather than being rewritten.

build where only a dependency changed (e.g. a newer @typetorch/framework)

commit.message:
Merge duplicate tags and normalise tags on input

The tag list had spelling and translation variants side by side
(coop/co-op, platform/platforms/plaftorm/platformer, aventure/adventure,
shoot'em'up/shoot 'em up…), and input was only split, trimmed and lower-
cased: a trailing comma could add an empty tag and a repeated tag made
the save fail on the game_tag key.

- Migration: a tag_alias table, and merge_tag_variant(variant, canonical),
  which moves a variant's games to the canonical tag (once), deletes it
  and keeps it as an alias. It merges the pairs agreed on #207 (roguelite
  and shoot 'em up stay separate genres) and deletes nameless tags.
- Input: tags are normalised (case, spaces, apostrophes, "'em"), empty
  and repeated ones dropped, and aliases mapped to their tag, on game
  create and edit.

Fixes #207.

commit.message:
Give every page its own description and share image

React Router 7 doesn't merge a route's meta with its parent's, so pages
that only set a title (/games) had no description at all, the homepage,
/about and /events shared the events tagline, game and org pages built
`${about}.` ("." or "null." when empty), and only detail pages with an
image had one when shared.

pageMeta() builds the whole set in one place: title, description, Open
Graph (type, site name, absolute URL, image) and Twitter tags, with the
large card whenever there is an image. summarize() turns an "about" into
a description (Markdown stripped, one line, cut at a word around 160
characters, never just punctuation). Every public route uses them:
- list pages each get their own description;
- game, org and event pages use their about, else a generated sentence
  ("Indie game by X, tagged Y.", "Video game studio in Rennes, FR.",
  the event's date and place);
- pages without their own image share public/og-default.png, rendered
  from the logo.

The charset and viewport tags stay in Layout only.

Fixes #196.

commit.message:
Show and enter event times in the event's own time zone

Event dates were formatted with whatever locale and time zone the code ran
in: cards in the viewer's (12-hour, no year), the event page in English
24-hour, so server and browser disagreed (#183's hydration errors) and
visitors abroad saw their own clock. The form sent wall-clock times
without an offset and the server read them in its own zone, so on a UTC
host every edit from France would have shifted the event.

- event.time_zone (IANA, default Europe/Paris), set from the location's
  coordinates on create and edit (offline lookup).
- eventTime.js: one formatter (en, 24-hour, year only when not the
  current one, plain spaces, hand-built ranges) and zone-aware
  conversion for datetime-local values; nothing depends on the process'
  time zone. Cards, the date label, the event page, its meta
  description and the game page's event list use it, and the form
  shows and reads times in the event's zone.
- <time dateTime> attributes used Date#toString (process time zone):
  now ISO strings.
- e2e runs the server in UTC.
- scripts/backfill-event-time-zones.mjs sets existing events' zones and
  re-reads their times as typed (saved as Europe/Paris), dry run first.

Fixes #204.

- surf rides in with a wash and the shore's foam flares;
- sparkles, crests of light, river streaks and flecks of foam, rings on
